newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ stands by easy credit amid growing optimism.
newsitem.headline: BOJ stands by easy credit amid growing optimism.

text.p: Growing expressions of optimism among politicians and bureaucrats about Japan's economic health have not convinced the Bank of Japan (BOJ) that the time has come to raise interest rates, senior money traders say.

"No matter what other policy-makers say, the BOJ's judgment is still that the economy is not sturdy enough to do without its shot in the arm (of ample liquidity)," said Tadao Sakashima, assistant general manager of the bond department at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.

In a surprise move, the BOJ, Japan's central bank, kept the money market awash in cash on Wednesday by providing 100 billion yen ($787 million) in fresh funds to the market, although it already had an ample surplus of 180 billion yen ($1.41 billion).
The action signalled the BOJ's strong desire to hold down rates, not just for the sake of the economy but to help out the troubled banking sector and weak stock market, traders said.
The central bank's ample fund injection comes at a time when various government officials have been making upbeat remarks about the state of the Japanese economy.

"The Japanese economy is now on an upward trend... The upside risk for the economy is higher than the downside risk. The Japanese people themselves must now realise the possibility (of the upside risk)," Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, was quoted by the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper as saying on Wednesday.
He also said it would be natural for stock prices in Japan to rise given that the economy had moved forward.

On Tuesday, cabinet minister Kabun Muto, head of the Management and Coordination Agency, said he had asked BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita to consider the possibility of raising the official discount rate, which the central bank charges on overnight loans to commercial banks.
Muto said Japan's money supply growth has been slow and that this can be explained by the outflow of Japanese funds into higher-yielding assets overseas.

Economists, however, attribute the slow money growth to write-offs of bad loans at Japan's commercial banks, which have soaked up liquidity inside the banking sector and prevented funds from flowing into the real economy. Japan's ultra-low interest rates are mostly aimed at facilitating bad loan write-offs by banks and corporations, they said.
Japan's money supply grew 3.0 percent year-on-year in February, at the lower end of economists' expectations.

"A lot depends on whether the government will be able to address the bad loan problems of the banking sector and construction companies by putting in place effective industrial policies and not abusing monetary policy," said Yoshiichi Taguchi, strategist at Tokio Marine MC Asset Management Co Ltd.

On the technical front, traders said the ample fund injection on Wednesday reflected the BOJ's intention to stand by its previous pledge to not allow the key call rate -- which banks charge each other for overnight funds -- to move above the discount rate on average. The pledge has been in place since September 8, 1995, when the BOJ cut the discount rate to a record low 0.5 percent.
The call rate, after rising as high as 0.72 percent, has been sticking to high levels in recent days, threatening the BOJ with the possibility of having to break that pledge.
"The central bank is bound to its pledge and this has led to its excessive fund injection, low interest rates and a weak yen," said Shin Nagai, a money market manager at ABN AMRO Bank.

Nagai said: "The overall economy is not so weak that it warrants the BOJ's massive liquidity supply, but lingering worries over the banking sector and weak stocks have given it a good excuse to hold down rates." ($1=127 yen)
